newsitem.title: FRANCE: France seeks benchmark role for Paris.
newsitem.headline: France seeks benchmark role for Paris.

text.p: France, underlining its commitment to European monetary union, said on Tuesday it had decided on how to convert government debt from francs to euros at the launch of a single currency in 1999.

French Treasury head Jean Lemierre told a business conference France would also issue new Treasury bills in euros on January 4, 1999, in what could be Europe's first government issue in the new currency.

The plans are meant to ensure Paris does not lose financial market business to London and Frankfurt after 1999, by trying to make French bonds a benchmark for the big new euro-denominated bond market which will emerge under monetary union.

Head of the French stock exchanges association (SBF) Jean-Francois Theodore also told the conference France was working with Germany and Switzerland to launch Europe-wide and euro-zone stock indices soon.
Officials said the indices were meant to compete with joint pan-European indices being set up by the London and Amsterdam stock exchanges.
Lemierre said France's stock of French franc-denominated debt would be converted into euros the same weekend that the single currency is launched.

The Treasury also said on Tuesday it would be selling, starting with its July 17 auction, Treasury notes (BTANs) with the same characteristics in francs and Ecus to allow the two bonds to be interchangeable after the introduction of the euro.
Government bond issues will be rounded to the nearest euro, and any extra value left over from the conversion will be repaid in cash, Lemierre said.
The exchange rate between francs and euros will run to five decimal places, meaning that without rounding, investors would be left with bond issues in unmanageable numbers.
Conversion of the stock of government debt into euros is seen by France as a key element in ensuring that the launch of the single currency is irreversible.

France has also drawn up a timetable for issuing new debt in euros, with the sale of bills due on January 4, and auctions planned on January 7 and 21 for the sale of bonds (OATs) and notes (BTANs) respectively.
"It is clear that our aim as an issuer is to play a role as a reference in the euro bond market," Lemierre said.
"The French Treasury bond is a good candidate to become a benchmark," Gerard Pfauwadel, head of the MATIF futures exchange, said.

France is hoping that its bond market, already highly liquid with issues which are easily interchangeable, can be used as the point of reference for all European government issues in euro-denominated debt.
France led the drive for early conversion of the stock of debt into euros.
Germany, whose banks feared being left behind by the French move, has just decided to convert its own stock of debt from January 1, 1999 as well.
Juergen Stark, state secretary in the German finance ministry, said on Tuesday that Finance Minister Theo Waigel had agreed to his proposal on early conversion of debt.
But though France seems to be stealing a march on dealings in the bond market, traditionally its speciality, its relatively small stock market is struggling to find a role for itself.
Plans to launch a joint stock trading system with German futures exchange DTB fell apart last year, though Pfauwadel said there was still scope for a new and different type of agreement.
This would involve connecting the two different systems rather than running French and German cash and derivatives trading on the same systems.
